subsection: 3. Case study: Lyndon Johnson and Vietnam, 1963–1968

notes.h: Background: the Cold War commitment Johnson inherited
notes.b: Johnson did not start the American involvement in Vietnam. He inherited a commitment built up over two earlier presidencies, driven by Cold War fear of communist expansion.
points: Containment was the Cold War policy of stopping communism spreading. In 1954 Eisenhower put forward the domino theory: if one country fell to communism its neighbours would fall one after another, like a row of dominoes. This is why Americans thought South Vietnam mattered so much.

The United States gave aid to France in its war in Vietnam and then to South Vietnam directly. Vietnam was divided in 1954 at the 17th parallel (a line of latitude), which left a communist state in the North and a US-backed state in the South.
Ho Chi Minh, a communist, led North Vietnam, and Ngo Dinh Diem led South Vietnam with American support. Diem's government was weak, which is why it needed outside help to survive.

The Viet Cong were communist guerrillas (fighters who use ambush and hit-and-run rather than open battle) operating inside South Vietnam against Diem's government. They were separate from the North Vietnamese Army, the regular army of the North.

Kennedy raised the number of US military advisers from under 1,000 in 1961 to about 16,000 by late 1963, but he sent no combat troops. So the United States was committed to South Vietnam's survival without yet fighting the war itself.

The Great Society was Johnson's domestic programme of civil rights, the War on Poverty, health and education. He announced it in May 1964, and it is the reason he wanted Vietnam kept in the background.
notes.tip: Don't mix up the Viet Cong (guerrillas in the South) with the North Vietnamese Army. Say which one you mean when you describe the enemy.

notes.h: Background: Johnson's career and political skills
notes.b: Johnson came to the presidency as one of the most skilful legislators in American history. His methods worked on Congress but not on an enemy abroad, which helps to explain why Vietnam beat him.
points: Lyndon Baines Johnson was born on 27 August 1908 near Stonewall, Texas. He became Texas director of the National Youth Administration (a New Deal agency that gave work to young people) in 1935 and was elected to the House of Representatives in 1937.
He won the 1948 Democratic Senate runoff in Texas by only 87 votes, which earned him the mocking nickname Landslide Lyndon. He took his Senate seat in January 1949.
He became Democratic leader in the Senate in 1953 and Majority Leader from 1955 to 1961. After losing the 1960 Democratic nomination to Kennedy he accepted the vice presidency (1961 to 1963).
He was a master of Senate politics and persuasion, using personal pressure on colleagues (the Johnson treatment) to pass legislation. This worked because colleagues needed his favour.
He could not apply those methods to a war against an enemy who would not bargain on his terms, because Hanoi had nothing to gain from his favour and could simply refuse to negotiate.
Kennedy was shot in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and Johnson was sworn in as president the same day. He remained president until January 1969.
notes.tip: A good answer on his leadership says what Johnson was good at (getting laws through Congress) and then why that skill failed in Vietnam.

notes.h: What Johnson inherited and why he kept to it
notes.b: Johnson took over a war that was going badly, in a country with an unstable government. He chose continuity, and his own fears of political damage made him hold on.
points: Diem was overthrown by a military coup on 1 to 2 November 1963 and killed, so the Saigon government was unstable when Johnson took office. The Viet Cong controlled large parts of the countryside, and about 16,000 US advisers were in the country.
Within days Johnson told his ambassador in Saigon that he would not lose Vietnam. National Security Action Memorandum 273 (26 November 1963) confirmed the policy of supporting South Vietnam.

He kept Kennedy's advisers: Robert McNamara (Secretary of Defense), Dean Rusk (Secretary of State) and McGeorge Bundy (national security adviser, replaced by Walt Rostow in 1966). So the same thinking about the war carried on.
Johnson feared that losing Vietnam would repeat the loss of China, when Truman's party had been attacked as soft on communism. He feared a right-wing backlash that would wreck his domestic programme.

He also believed that losing South Vietnam would damage US credibility worldwide, because other allies would doubt American promises. He was a firm anti-communist who was also aware of the domestic cost of war.
notes.tip: For 'why did Johnson escalate', give four linked causes: the inherited commitment, fear of being blamed for a 'loss', Cold War credibility and protecting the Great Society.

notes.h: The Gulf of Tonkin and the 1964 election
notes.b: Two incidents in the Gulf of Tonkin gave Johnson congressional authority for a larger war, and the 1964 election confirmed his mandate while he presented himself as the candidate of restraint.
points: On 2 August 1964 North Vietnamese torpedo boats attacked the US destroyer USS Maddox, which was on a naval intelligence patrol near the North Vietnamese coast. South Vietnamese raids on that coast (Operation 34A) had taken place days before, and Hanoi linked them to the patrol.

A second attack reported on 4 August 1964, on the Maddox and the destroyer USS Turner Joy, is now believed not to have happened. Sonar and radar readings in bad weather were misread, and later documents showed that officials doubted the report even as it was used.
On the evening of 4 August Johnson announced retaliation, and air strikes hit North Vietnamese naval bases on 5 August.

The Tonkin Gulf Resolution, passed on 7 August 1964 by 416 votes to 0 in the House and 88 to 2 in the Senate, authorised the President to take 'all necessary measures'. This gave Johnson a free hand without a declaration of war.

Senator J. William Fulbright helped steer it through the Senate. Senators Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening voted against it. A draft resolution had been prepared before the incidents, and critics later argued that Johnson used the doubtful second incident to obtain it.

In the election of 3 November 1964 Johnson won about 61 per cent of the popular vote against Barry Goldwater, who had called for stronger action in Vietnam and was portrayed as reckless. Johnson presented himself as the candidate of restraint.

The restraint was a political strategy. Johnson publicly promised not to widen the war while privately preparing for a larger one, which is the gap between campaign promises and later action that critics later seized on.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: the real attack on 2 August, the doubtful one on 4 August, the Resolution on 7 August. Quote the votes (416 to 0 and 88 to 2) when asked about the Resolution.

notes.h: Escalation: Flaming Dart, Rolling Thunder and the first combat troops, early 1965
notes.b: In the first months of 1965 Johnson moved from reprisal to a sustained bombing campaign and then to ground troops. This turned an advisers' war into an American war.
points: On 7 February 1965 a Viet Cong attack on the American base at Pleiku killed eight Americans. Johnson ordered reprisal air raids (Flaming Dart), which led on to sustained bombing.

Operation Rolling Thunder, a sustained bombing campaign against North Vietnam, began on 2 March 1965 and continued in stages until 2 November 1968. Its aims were to put pressure on Hanoi and to support the Saigon government.

Its limit was that bombing did not stop the war. North Vietnam refused to negotiate while the bombing continued, and the Viet Cong kept fighting in the South, supplied through the Ho Chi Minh Trail (a network of routes through Laos and Cambodia).
About 3,500 US Marines landed at Da Nang on 8 March 1965, the first American ground combat troops in Vietnam. They were sent to protect the air base, but they began the build-up of ground forces.

Johnson's strategy was to hold the South while signalling willingness to negotiate. In his Johns Hopkins University speech in Baltimore on 7 April 1965 he offered unconditional discussions and a development plan for the Mekong region (about one billion dollars).
Hanoi did not accept, so the offer of talks was not followed up, and the build-up went on.
notes.tip: Don't confuse Flaming Dart (reprisal raids, February 1965) with Rolling Thunder (sustained bombing from 2 March 1965), or the Johns Hopkins peace offer (7 April) with the 28 July troop announcement.

notes.h: The July 1965 decision, troop numbers and the low-key escalation
notes.b: Johnson committed large ground forces in the summer of 1965, but he did it quietly and against some advice. He wanted to protect the Great Society legislation then passing through Congress.
points: General William Westmoreland, commander of US forces from June 1964, argued that a war of attrition with large forces would wear down the North Vietnamese.

Johnson's advisers were not united. Under Secretary of State George Ball argued in memos in 1964 and 1965 that the United States would be dragged into an unwinnable land war, but Johnson, McNamara, Rusk and Bundy chose escalation.

On 28 July 1965 Johnson announced that US forces would rise from 75,000 to 125,000 at once and that more would follow as commanders requested. He asked for no declaration of war and did not call up the reserves.
He kept the escalation low-key and avoided a formal declaration of war because he did not want to endanger his Great Society legislation, which was passing through Congress in 1965.

US troop numbers were about 184,000 at the end of 1965, about 385,000 at the end of 1966 and about 485,000 at the end of 1967. They were over 500,000 in 1968 and peaked at about 540,000 in 1969 before falling.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the escalation was gradual and low-key. Answer with the Great Society, no call-up of reserves and no declaration of war. Use the troop figures by year to show the scale.

notes.h: Westmoreland's strategy and the war on the ground
notes.b: Westmoreland's methods turned the war into a contest of firepower and numbers. They killed many people but did not break communist will, and they carried heavy costs for Vietnamese civilians and Americans alike.
points: Westmoreland's strategy was attrition (wearing the enemy down by killing more than they could replace) through search and destroy. Large units hunted communist forces in the countryside, using helicopters, artillery and air power, and success was measured by the body count.

Attrition failed because the communists could choose when to fight and replaced losses from a large population and from supplies carried down the Ho Chi Minh Trail. So the killing did not break their will.

Heavy firepower, including napalm (a sticky burning fuel) and the defoliant Agent Orange (a chemical that strips leaves so the enemy cannot hide), killed civilians and drove peasants into government-controlled camps or towards the Viet Cong.

Pacification (winning over the countryside) and the building of a stable South Vietnamese government lagged behind. The Saigon regime was led by generals, and Nguyen Van Thieu became president in September 1967 after elections criticised as flawed.
In November 1967 Westmoreland told Washington that the end was in view. This set up the shock of the Tet Offensive.
On 16 March 1968 American soldiers killed several hundred unarmed villagers at My Lai. The massacre was exposed publicly in November 1969.

More than 30,000 Americans were dead by the end of 1968. The draft (compulsory military service) gave deferments to most college students, so it fell on those without them and spread the war's costs through American families.
notes.tip: When asked why attrition failed, name the cause and its effect: the enemy chose the battle, had the manpower and the Ho Chi Minh Trail, so body counts did not show who was winning.

notes.h: The credibility gap and the anti-war movement
notes.b: As the war grew, Johnson's public statements were increasingly doubted. From 1965 his critics in Congress, universities, churches and the press challenged the war.
points: Journalists used the term credibility gap from the mid-1960s for the gap between official statements on the war and what reporters found in Vietnam. Johnson played the war down in public to protect the Great Society, so the later gap between his optimism and events hurt him.
The first teach-in (a meeting of lectures and debate against the war) was held at the University of Michigan on 24 to 25 March 1965. Student and church opposition grew steadily through 1966 and 1967.
Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) led a march of about 20,000 in Washington on 17 April 1965.

Senator J. William Fulbright, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, held televised hearings in February 1966 that questioned the war's basis. He had helped steer the 1964 resolution through, so his change of mind carried weight.
His book The Arrogance of Power (1966) argued that the United States was acting as a great power imposing its will on a small nation.
On 4 April 1967 Martin Luther King spoke against the war in his Beyond Vietnam speech at Riverside Church, New York, linking the war to poverty and racism.
On 28 April 1967 Muhammad Ali refused induction into the army in Houston and was stripped of his heavyweight title, which made the draft a public issue.
On 21 October 1967 about 50,000 people marched on the Pentagon, showing that opposition had spread well beyond students.
notes.tip: For a source question on a speech, cartoon or critic's account, place it first by date, speaker and purpose. Fulbright (1966) and King (1967) are the usual critics, and King's speech is dated 4 April 1967, a year to the day before his death.

notes.h: The arguments over the war: imperialism, public opinion and the military-industrial complex
notes.b: By 1967 Americans were arguing about why the country was in Vietnam at all. Three ideas shaped the argument: that the war was imperialism, that opinion was turning, and that defence interests drove it.
points: Imperialism was the critics' charge that a great power was imposing its will on a small nation. Fulbright used this argument, and it challenged the claim that the United States was only defending a free people.

Critics argued that the war was costly and immoral and was draining money and attention from the Great Society. They also argued that the war was a civil war in which Americans had no right to intervene.
Supporters argued that withdrawal would damage America's credibility abroad and that the domino theory meant that other countries would fall if South Vietnam did.

The military-industrial complex was the interest shared by defence contractors, the armed forces and government in high defence spending. Eisenhower had warned of it in his farewell address on 17 January 1961, and critics linked it to the war.

Public opinion means the views of ordinary Americans, measured by polls and shaped by television and the press. It had turned against the war and Johnson from 1967, and by late 1967 Johnson's approval was about 40 per cent or below.
notes.tip: When you write about public opinion, name the evidence that shows how far it had turned, such as the polls of late 1967 and the Pentagon march, rather than saying only that people were unhappy.

notes.h: The costs to the Great Society
notes.b: Johnson tried to fund both the war and his domestic programme, and the cost of the war weakened his reform agenda.
points: The Great Society's biggest laws came first: the Civil Rights Act (2 July 1964), Medicare and Medicaid (July 1965) and the Voting Rights Act (6 August 1965). They were passed before the war's costs became acute, and they are Johnson's most secure achievements.
Johnson tried to pay for the war and the Great Society together, a policy critics called guns and butter. He delayed asking Congress for a tax increase until January 1967.
Federal deficits grew and inflation rose after 1965, passing 4 per cent in 1968. Congress passed a 10 per cent income tax surcharge in June 1968 to restrain spending.
The War on Poverty (declared January 1964) was cut or diverted as military spending grew, so many programmes were underfunded as they expanded.

Urban riots, such as Watts in 1965 and Detroit in 1967, added to the loss of support. By 1967 the war's rising cost and the riots had turned public opinion against new domestic spending, so the Great Society lost momentum.
notes.tip: To show how Vietnam affected his presidency, link cause to effect: war spending, deficits and inflation, loss of support for domestic spending. Don't just list the programmes.

notes.h: Tet, the 1968 turning point and Johnson's withdrawal
notes.b: The Tet Offensive of January 1968 did not defeat the Americans militarily, but it shattered their optimism and ended Johnson's chance of re-election.
points: Tet began on 30 January 1968 (the night of 30 to 31 January), during the Tet holiday. Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces attacked more than a hundred towns and cities across South Vietnam, including Saigon and Hue, which was retaken after about a month of fighting.
On 31 January a Viet Cong squad entered the US embassy compound in Saigon and held out for about six hours. Television pictures shocked American opinion, even though the communists failed to hold it.

Militarily Tet was a heavy defeat for the communists, who lost very heavily, the Viet Cong especially. Politically it was an American defeat, because Westmoreland had said in November 1967 that the end was in view, so Tet looked like proof that official optimism was false.
On 27 February 1968 the television newsman Walter Cronkite broadcast a report calling the war a stalemate. It was widely reported as a sign of changing opinion.
In February 1968 Westmoreland and the Joint Chiefs asked for about 206,000 more troops. Clark Clifford, who became Secretary of Defense on 1 March 1968 when McNamara left, advised against it.
The Wise Men (senior outside advisers) told Johnson in late March that the war could not be won at an acceptable cost.
In the New Hampshire primary on 12 March 1968 the anti-war Democrat Eugene McCarthy ran Johnson close. Robert Kennedy entered the race in mid-March, so Johnson was weakened within his own party.

On 31 March 1968 Johnson announced a partial halt to the bombing north of the 20th parallel, offered talks and said he would not seek re-election. Peace talks began in Paris in May, but the war continued.

Martin Luther King was assassinated on 4 April 1968. Robert Kennedy was shot on 5 June and died on 6 June. Rioting between police and protesters marked the Democratic convention in Chicago in August. Hubert Humphrey lost narrowly to Richard Nixon in November.
notes.tip: Say that Tet was a communist military defeat but an American political defeat. Don't mix Eugene McCarthy (anti-war Democrat) with Joe McCarthy, or McNamara with Clifford or Robert Kennedy.

notes.b: A huge American effort failed to defeat a determined enemy. Historians and contemporaries give several linked reasons, and the best answers back each with evidence.
points: The war was a limited one. The US avoided invading North Vietnam, mining Haiphong harbour (the North's main port) or using nuclear weapons, partly from fear of bringing in China or the Soviet Union, and this limited the pressure on Hanoi.

North Vietnam and the Viet Cong used bases in Laos and Cambodia and the Ho Chi Minh Trail, which the US was reluctant to attack. So they could withdraw and rebuild, and their determination did not break.
The South Vietnamese government was weak and corrupt, and the Army of the Republic of Vietnam could not hold the territory cleared by American forces.
The strategy of attrition and the body count measure were criticised within the US army and in the press as misleading about the progress of the war.

Johnson's gradual escalation and his refusal to consider a clear withdrawal kept options open while costs and divisions at home grew. He never explained clear aims to the public, so home support drained away.
Historians differ on the cause. Some say Johnson was trapped by the assumptions of the Cold War, while others argue that he made avoidable choices on escalation in 1964 and 1965.
notes.tip: Aim for four or five distinct reasons, each with evidence: limited war, enemy sanctuaries and determination, a weak Saigon, flawed strategy, and loss of support at home.

notes.b: Johnson was the president who made Vietnam an American war and also the president of the Great Society. He was a decision-maker at the centre of events, not a witness.
points: His career: House of Representatives 1937, Senate 1949, Majority Leader 1955 to 1961, vice president 1961 to 1963, and president from 22 November 1963 to January 1969.
His domestic record was one of the greatest legislative achievements of any president: the Civil Rights Act (1964), the Voting Rights Act (1965), Medicare, Medicaid and federal aid to education.
In Vietnam he took the decisions of 1964 and 1965 to bomb North Vietnam and send combat troops, always in steps. He hoped to avoid a wider war with China or the Soviet Union, as in Korea in 1950.

He shaped events by making those decisions and was shaped by them. The Tet shock and falling support forced him out in 1968, and protesters outside the White House chanted at him about how many children he had killed that day.

Contemporaries saw him as a forceful, domineering leader who was crude, devious and driven. The credibility gap made many doubt his word, though supporters pointed to his achievements for the poor and for black Americans.
Historians in the 1970s, such as the journalist David Halberstam in The Best and the Brightest (1972), blamed the arrogance of the advisers he inherited.

Later historians, such as Robert Dallek in Flawed Giant (1998) and Fredrik Logevall in Choosing War (1999), stress that Johnson had alternatives in 1964 and 1965 and chose escalation, partly to protect his domestic reputation.
notes.tip: Name Halberstam against Dallek and Logevall to show that historians disagree about whether the advisers or Johnson made the choice. It adds weight to a judgement.

notes.b: Examiners reward a clear judgement, stated at the start, that weighs Johnson's domestic achievements against his failure in Vietnam and sets contemporary views against later ones.
points: Success at home: the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, Medicare and Medicaid are judged to be major achievements of twentieth-century social reform, passed in 1964 and 1965.
Failure abroad: the United States did not win in Vietnam, and about 58,000 Americans died in the whole war. The war damaged the Great Society and the public's trust in government.

Contemporaries were divided. In 1964 and 1965 most Americans admired him as a strong, effective leader, but by late 1967 his approval had fallen to about 40 per cent or below. Protesters chanted about how many children he had killed that day.

Later historians disagree. Halberstam blamed the arrogant advisers, while Dallek and Logevall argue that Johnson made avoidable choices. The debate is whether he was trapped by Cold War assumptions or chose escalation.

Overall he was a great domestic president whose war undermined his presidency. The credibility gap was his lasting legacy, a problem of trust between president and public that continued to shape politics after Vietnam.
notes.tip: State your verdict in the first lines of an essay on how successful Johnson was, then balance achievements and failures with dates and finish with an overall judgement.

keyTerms.definition: The resolution of 7 August 1964 by which Congress authorised the President to take all necessary measures in Vietnam, giving Johnson wide war powers.
The sustained US bombing campaign against North Vietnam, which began on 2 March 1965.
The difference, widely noticed from 1965, between the official government account of the Vietnam War and what was reported from the war zone.
The coordinated communist attacks across South Vietnam beginning on 30 January 1968, which shattered American confidence in official optimism.
Johnson's programme of domestic reform, which included civil rights, health and education laws, and the War on Poverty.
The view of ordinary Americans, measured by polls and reported by the media, which turned against the war and against Johnson from 1967.
The critics' term for the US role in Vietnam, arguing that an outside power was imposing its will on a small nation.
The network of defence contractors, the armed forces and government agencies whose shared interests promoted high defence spending, a phrase popularised by Eisenhower in 1961.
Westmoreland's tactic of sending large American units to find and kill communist forces in the countryside, with progress measured by the body count.
The policy of paying for the Vietnam War and the Great Society at the same time, without raising taxes at first, which fed inflation.
The strategy of inflicting losses on the enemy faster than it could replace them, in the hope that Hanoi would give up.
Conscription under which young men could be called into the army, with deferments for most college students, which fuelled the anti-war movement.
